I just spent three hours on the DSA lab exam, wrote a working solution, but then deleted the whole thing in the last 10 minutes because I convinced myself it was too simple and must have missed an edge case. I do this every single time, I literally cannot trust my own brain even when the code is literally running fine on my screen.

Had my placement interview today and it actually went okay, but now I'm lying in bed replaying every single word I said. I keep thinking, 'Why did I say that? The interviewer looked at me weird. I had to lock in my specialization stream tonight, and I chose AI over Web Dev, but the second I hit submit, my chest went tight. What if I can't handle the math? What if Web Dev had better placement packages? I've been opening and closing the registration portal for six hours trying to mail the admin to change it back, but then I think no, what if AI is better? I feel like I'm literally paralyzing myself because I can't trust any decision I make.

I sent a draft of our final year project proposal to our guide, and he replied with 'Okay, let's meet tomorrow.' That's it. Just four words. I've read those four words fifty times. Does 'Okay' mean he thinks it's trash? Did I sound arrogant in my email? Should I have rewritten the methodology section before sending? I'm so tempted to send an apology email right now explaining why the draft is so rough, but my group partner told me to stop being crazy.

We had a group study session for the upcoming gate exam today, and I suggested a shortcut for a calculus problem. Everyone just went quiet for a second before the group topper said 'yeah, that works too' and moved on. Now I can't stop thinking I sounded like an idiot who was just trying to show off. I've literally been sitting here for two hours replaying their facial expressions, wishing I had just kept my mouth shut and stayed quiet like I usually do.

I was in the DSA lab today, and my code actually compiled on the first run. Instead of just clicking submit, I sat there staring at the screen, convinced I'd missed some massive edge case because there was no way I got it right so fast. I started rewriting the logic, overcomplicating the loops, and wound up running out of time before I could submit anything at all. I literally had the working solution right in front of me and I ruined it because I can't trust my own brain for five seconds.

I just got my DBMS midterm paper back and I want to scream at myself. I originally ticked the correct options for three of the trickiest SQL queries, but in the last five minutes of the exam, my hands started shaking and I convinced myself my first instincts were too simple to be right. I crossed them all out and wrote the wrong answers, and now those missed marks are going to tank my GPA. If I had just left my paper alone, I'd be fine, but I always find a way to become my own biggest enemy.

I spent three hours drafting a simple Slack message to my project guide asking for a two-day extension on our system design document. I rewrote it about forty times, asking myself if 'Dear Professor' sounded too clinical or if 'Hi' was too casual, and wondering if he'd think I'm just lazy. I finally hit send, and now I'm literally staring at my screen, sweating, wishing I could pull the message back because I’m convinced he’s going to think I’m an absolute joke of a student.

During the placement prep group discussion today, the coordinator asked how to optimize a database architecture. I had the exact answer written down in my notebook, but I kept telling myself, 'There's no way it's that easy, you probably misunderstanding the question.' Then this guy next to me says literally word-for-word what I wrote, and the mentor praised him for his 'brilliant approach.' Why do I always assume everyone else in the room is inherently smarter than me?

I got an offer from a mid-tier tech firm yesterday, which is great because so many of my batchmates are still unplaced. But instead of feeling relieved, I've spent the last 24 hours in a complete spiral, wondering if I settled too quickly and if I should have held out for the product-based companies next month. I can't even celebrate my own win because my brain keeps screaming that I’ve made a massive mistake that’s going to ruin my entire career trajectory.
Every time I want to speak in class, I spent the rest of the time second-guessing and changing correct answers to wrong ones. I'm paralyzing myself with this constant doubt.

I had the working solution for the graph traversal problem in today's DSA lab 20 minutes before the end of the session. Now I ended up with a compilation error, a big fat zero, and I'm sitting in the washroom stall literally wanting to claw my face off because I can't even trust my own working code.

I was in the technical round for an internship today and the interviewer asked me about database indexing. I knew the correct answer instantly, but as I started speaking, I saw him squint his eyes slightly and my brain went into absolute overdrive. I immediately backtracked, apologized, and mumbled some completely wrong alternative theory just to appease him. I found out later my first answer was 100% correct, and now I'm lying in bed staring at the ceiling, utterly sickened by how easily I override my own brain the second someone looks at me weird.

I spent forty-five minutes drafting a question for our operating systems discussion board because I was genuinely stuck on thread synchronization. I instantly felt like an absolute fraud, assumed my question would make the professor think I'm too dumb for this course, and deleted the whole draft.
